title: An Easy Way To Build Rapport Online (Or In Class) https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/09/26/an-easy-way-to-build-rapport-online-or-in-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin revisits an older rapport-building strategy — leaving short, individual notes for students after class — and argues it translates especially well to remote teaching, where cameras-off policies can leave a teacher facing a wall of blank screens. He specifies three criteria for an effective note: uniqueness, meaning it avoids generic praise language like 'good job' and instead names something specific the student said or did; specificity, meaning it names a talent or trait the student may not even realize they have; and honesty, since students can detect insincerity and trust erodes once they catch a teacher exaggerating. He argues that in a generation desensitized to flattery, this kind of individualized, honest attention is what actually reaches students and builds influence.
points: Leave short, individual notes for students after class via email, Remind, or the Google Classroom stream.
Avoid generic praise language like 'good job'; instead reference something specific the student said or did.
Name a talent or strength the student may not realize they have — specificity is what makes a note influential.
Notes must be honest; students can detect insincerity, and a caught exaggeration damages trust permanently.
This strategy is especially valuable when cameras-off policies prevent teachers from building rapport visually.
quotes: It’s to leave short, personal notes for individual students after class has ended.
Avoid trite language like “good-job” and “way-to-go,” which have lost their meaning due to overuse. Now they make students feel as if they’re just another face in the crowd.
Specificity is the key to finding the most influential words to put in your message. Focus on things your students would never in a million years think anyone would notice.
Kids these days are more aware than we think and can identify a phony from a mile away. So whatever you write in your note, make sure it’s honest.
In this way, you build your reputation as someone who can be trusted—which is crucial to having influential, behavior-changing relationships with even the most challenging students.
This generation, world-weary and jaded in so many ways even before Covid, shrug in the face of flattery and compliments that made students blush not ten years ago.
